newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Clarke should act on rates - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Clarke should act on rates - analysts.

text.p: Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke should heed the warnings from the central bank and raise rates to 6.25 percent at the forthcoming March 5 monetary meeting, a growing number of analysts say.

"Clarke should take notice of the Bank of England's warnings on interest rates and put them up at the next monetary meeting to keep inflation in check," Neil Parker, treasury economist at the Royal Bank of Scotland said.

The bank's quarterly inflation report published on Wednesday argued that money and demand growth in the British economy was not compatible with the government hitting its ambitious 2.5 percent inflation target.

The bank, led by inflation hawk Eddie George, is calling for a pre-emptive hike in rates to at least 6.25 percent, to help reduce core inflation which stands at 3.1 percent and check a sharp rise in consumer spending.

"The bank's central projection for inflation two years ahead is close to three percent and rising," it said in its report. "In the light of the central projection and the risks surrounding it, the bank continues to see the need for a moderate tightening of policy."
Britain's central bank has painful memories of the 1980s spending boom, when inflation ran out of control and rose above 10 percent, after failure to raise rates early enough in the economic cycle.

Chancellor Clarke, mindful of the forthcoming election which must be held by May 22, has argued the bank's analysis of the inflation risk is wrong, not least because sterling's 16 percent rise since August will help keep inflation in check.
But there is growing concern Clarke is loathe to raise rates ahead of the election because of the risk of alienating voters in a country where 67 percent own their homes.

In the last four years British interest rates have been at their lowest on a sustained basis since the early 1960s as part of the most dramatic loosening of policy since World War Two. But a growing number of economists believe Clarke has become too mesmerised by published inflation numbers and the election.

Many economists argue that British consumers are rediscovering their dangerous borrowing and spending ways of the 1980s boom, as retail sales volumes rise, consumer credit surges and house prices start to lift off.

And with consumers set to receive some 18 billion pounds in windfall payments from building societies (home loan groups) floating on the stock exchange later this year, economists say Clarke should raise rates now to dampen down demand.

"Interest rates are too low and should be at 6.25 percent. The bank is clearly recommending a pre-emptive move and a quarter point rise would be desirable at this stage, even though some other inflation indicators are flashing contrary signals on prices," said Jeremy Hawkins, economist at Bank America.

Analysts said a pre-emptive move would reassure financial markets that monetary policy was not being infected by political considerations and would help ensure Britain does not throw away its chance of strong and sustained, non-inflationary growth, which many European partners increasingly envy.

Many analysts back the Bank of England's contention that sterling's rally is no substitute for an interest rate rise, because cheaper import prices from a lower exchange rate may simply be used to fatten profit margins rather than be passed to consumers who have become less price-sensitive.
Wage growth, a bugbear in the economic boom/bust of the 1980s, is threatening to emerge as a problem. Figures on Wednesday showed average earnings at 4.25 percent, the highest for four years.
Economic growth, too, is set to accelerate this year to well above 3.0 percent, clearly in excess of the 2.25 percent average rate of expansion over the past four decades.
The Bank of England's chief economist Mervyn King told a news conference that the longer the delay in raising interest rates, the greater the increase would eventually have to be.
Despite the split over rates, analysts said the bank appeared to backtrack from its previous recommendation that a half point rise would be needed in the early part of 1997.
"This (the inflation report) is a far throw from the half point rise called for in the December monetary minutes (by the bank) said Alex Garrard, economist at Union Bank of Switzerland.
Garrard, unlike many other analysts, argues the bank's view on sterling and rates is too strong.
"Sterling (rise) has extended way beyond the bank's presumption that it would be temporary and not really matter, and the domestic sector looks like it is slowing of its own accord," he said.
